Same licenses.
Different work.

Thirteen stops follow fictional Parkside from its CEO’s confident view to the work people actually do. Parkside already pays for three company AI platforms and has four department agents, and the useful work still stays with each person. Then show what Nine-67 builds on those company tools, where it lives, who does what, and the steps to get there.

The setup

Parkside licenses Microsoft 365 Copilot for all 150 people, plus company Claude and ChatGPT plans. IT and departments built four Copilot Studio agents (Ask Parkside, Ask Ops, Ask Sales, Ask Service), each with its own sources and owner. Some people still use the personal ChatGPT, Grok or Perplexity they learned on first. The company, people and records are fictional.

How to present it

Josh drives the screens and narration. Suuchi explains what Nine-67 would discover and build. Keep one workspace or improvement in focus. Use the run of show below. The older scene notes further down are background only.

Run of show · 13 stops · about 21.5 minutes, then Q&A. Press → to advance. N shows the cue. Click any card on the graph to open someone not on the path.

  1. Dana’s view (1 min). Three company AI platforms and a live IT agent. Her confidence is reasonable.
  2. Research (2 min). 83% more productive, 69% private, 85% use vs. 29% embed. Different surveys.
  3. AI stack (2 min). 3 platforms, 4 agents, 3 personal apps, 0 connected.
  4. All 150 (1 min). 128 of 150, 111 company, 17 personal.
  5. Graph (1 min). Nine of them. Point at the four outlined, then go.
  6. Priya (2 min). Company Claude, still her own chats.
  7. Marcus (1.5 min). Company seat, still Grok from before the rollout. No blame.
  8. Elena (1.5 min). Struggling. Broad prompt, generic answer, back to manual.
  9. Leah (2 min). The glue. Every company tool, and she still stitches the week by hand. Read the band.
  10. Meet the Parkside AI Register (2 min). The Parkside AI Register in the middle. Around it, company tools built from each person’s real work on Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT. Green lines propose, blue lines read. Personal apps: we learn from them, never connect them. Close on how it works: a tool proposes, a named owner approves, it lands where people work.
  11. The AI Register we built, live for one week (2.5 min, 4 presses). Same four boxes every time, left to right: a tool proposes, the owner approves, a row lands in the Register, it shows up in that person’s tool. HF-01 shows the pattern; then Priya (REC-07), Elena’s agent proposing Nina (T-41, Nina approves), Marcus (CALL-12). Last press: the Friday Brief writes Leah’s draft from approved rows only.
  12. Connected (1.5 min). Same people, same AI. Every tool reads one Register; nothing counts until a named owner approves it. Personal apps are never connected.
  13. How we build it (1.5 min). Discover, prioritize, build, measure. Nine-67 builds with your people, your IT approves access, every tool has a named owner, leadership picks priorities. Then the CTA. Type “discovery” in the chat. Leave it up for Q&A.

Fix section (stops 10 to 12) totals about 6 minutes.

Q&A: What exactly gets built, where, and by whom?

One SharePoint list, the AI Register, in your Microsoft 365. Then one tool per workflow on the platform that person already uses: Copilot Studio agents (Project Tracker Assist, Friday Brief, plus one new action on Ask Ops), a shared Claude project (Month-End Reconciliation), and a company custom GPT (Call Prep Coach). Nine-67 engineers build them with the employees. IT approves access. Department owners review.

Q&A: Do we need new AI tools?

No. We build on the AI you already license: Copilot, Claude and ChatGPT company plans. Some connectors, such as HubSpot and Zendesk in Power Platform, are Premium and may need Power Platform licensing. We confirm that in discovery.

Q&A: Do Claude and ChatGPT write to SharePoint?

Not natively. They propose drafts through a connector IT approves. Claude reads company files through the Microsoft 365 connector IT enables.

Q&A: What about private chats and personal AI?

Never imported, read or connected. Personal accounts sit outside company admin control and business data terms. We ask people what works for them, they choose what to share, and we rebuild the best of it as a company tool. A shared Claude project does not expose anyone’s chats.

Q&A: What about the other 140 people?

The Register is where every new tool and agent plugs in. Shared tools spread: Maya runs Priya’s project. Discovery covers every department, and we start with the handoffs that touch the most people.

Q&A: Training on our data?

Company plans are covered by business data terms. Personal accounts are not. Verify current terms before quoting them.

Q&A: Why SharePoint? Will it scale?

It is already your system of record. If you outgrow it, move to Dataverse in the same tenant. Still no new vendor.

Q&A: How long and how much?

That comes out of the Discovery Session.

Q&A: Should we just standardize on one tool, or ban personal AI?

Leah, Ben, Ava and Elena all use the company Copilot and their work is still disconnected. More of one tool does not connect handoffs, and banning personal apps does not connect anything either. We build on the company tools, learn from what people figured out on their own, and only move reviewed business information between people.

Q&A: The other people on the map

Daniel, IT: Ask Parkside is one of four department agents in Copilot Studio, each with its own sources and owner. He approves every connector in the fix. Dana, CEO: Her company Claude board prep project starts from reviewed Register items, not hand-assembled decks.

Research and demonstration boundaries

Miro: State of Intelligent Collaboration 2026 supplies the 83% and 69% findings. Atlassian: State of Teams 2026 supplies the 85% and 29% findings. These are self-reported vendor surveys from different samples.

Parkside, its employees, workspaces and cases are fictional. All nine featured employees have company Copilot licenses, and Parkside also has company Claude and ChatGPT plans. The demo does not send messages, read private chats or personal accounts, or change live business records. It does not claim measured ROI or a production integration result.
